subject: Cloud Computing
title: SaaS Sprawl: Too Many Tools
description: A 60-second lesson on SaaS Sprawl: Too Many Tools.

hook.text: The average enterprise pays for 300+ SaaS subscriptions. Many are duplicates nobody tracks.

buildup.text: SaaS sprawl happens when departments buy tools independently without central coordination.

discovery.text: Shadow IT — tools adopted without IT approval — accounts for 40% of SaaS spending in many companies.

twist.text: Unused licenses waste billions globally. Studies show 25% of SaaS licenses go unused each month.

climax.text: SaaS management platforms now exist just to track and optimize all your other SaaS subscriptions.

punchline.text: There's now SaaS to manage your SaaS problem. Oh, the irony.

quiz.question: What is 'SaaS sprawl'?
options: Uncontrolled adoption of too many SaaS tools with overlapping functionality
A SaaS application that grows too large to function properly
When a SaaS company expands to too many countries

details.summary: SaaS sprawl occurs when organizations accumulate dozens or hundreds of overlapping subscriptions without centralized oversight. Duplicate tools waste money, fragment data, and create unmonitored security risks across shadow IT applications.
details.whyItMatters: The average enterprise uses over 100 SaaS tools, many adopted without IT approval. Sprawl wastes budget, fragments workflows, and expands the attack surface significantly.
takeaways: The average enterprise uses over 100 SaaS applications
Overlapping tools waste money and fragment workflows
Shadow IT creates unmonitored security risks

faq.question: How does SaaS sprawl happen?
faq.answer: Easy self-service sign-up and free tiers let employees adopt tools without IT involvement. Different teams buy overlapping tools independently. When no one tracks subscriptions centrally, costs accumulate and data becomes scattered across dozens of unmanaged platforms.

faq.question: How can SaaS sprawl be controlled?
faq.answer: Implement a SaaS management platform that discovers all subscriptions. Establish an approval workflow for new tools, consolidate overlapping products, negotiate enterprise agreements for widely used tools, and regularly audit unused licenses for cancellation.
